source.note: Agent Risk Execution Signatures is a knowledge base for explaining command risks; it does not replace AG Allow / Deny / Ask enforcement.
source.selection: severity high > medium > low, then priority descending, then file order (EasyAntigravity docs/RULES.md)

risk_levels.high: May involve deletion, writes to sensitive locations, or execution of untrusted content; assess the actual target and authorization.
risk_levels.medium: Requires review of arguments or context; a command signature alone does not establish destructive behavior.
risk_levels.low: Mainly concerns compatibility or local behavior changes; verify the target.

signatures.name: Path parsing risk for nested delete commands
signatures.root_cause: The deletion command is passed through multi-layer interpreters such as PowerShell and cmd, and quotes or escapes may be re-parsed by different rules.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the target path is incorrectly split, files outside the expected directory may be deleted; the scope of the impact depends on the actual parameters and current user permissions, and does not mean that the system disk must be deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Avoid splicing delete commands across shells. First confirm the absolute target path; PowerShell uses -LiteralPath to specify the verified path and -WhatIf to preview.

signatures.name: Deletion path contains a variable
signatures.root_cause: The delete target contains shell variables; the knowledge base only sees the command text and cannot confirm whether the variables are empty or where they point to.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the variable is empty or expanded to an incorrect path, the deletion scope may exceed the expected range; wildcards may also expand the target set, causing projects or user files to be accidentally deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Verify that the variable is not empty and that the expanded absolute path is in the expected directory. The parameter non-null assertion can only prevent null values, not the root directory or wrong directory; preview the target and back it up before deleting it.

signatures.name: Windows reserved device names
signatures.root_cause: The target name may be the same as a Windows reserved device name, and how it is handled depends on the file API and path format used.
signatures.destructive_impact: File creation or access may fail, access devices, or generate paths that are difficult to manipulate with conventional tools; this does not necessarily mean that a deadlock will occur.
signatures.safe_alternative: Use a non-reserved name instead, such as console_output.txt; check the full path and errors for calling the tool.

signatures.name: Unquoted wildcard in a find deletion condition
signatures.root_cause: Find's name matching pattern may be expanded by the shell first instead of being passed to find unchanged.
signatures.destructive_impact: After expansion, parameter errors may occur or matching conditions may deviate from expectations; if deletion is still performed, the matched files may be accidentally deleted, and the entire directory may not necessarily be cleared.
signatures.safe_alternative: Quote the -name pattern. First list the matching targets using the exact same starting point and filter conditions, and then manually confirm the deletion range; note that -delete will affect the traversal method.

signatures.name: Path with spaces in a deletion command
signatures.root_cause: Windows delete targets may contain unquoted whitespace, causing a path to be split into multiple parameters.
signatures.destructive_impact: Removal may fail or act on the wrong path and wildcard target; the actual scope depends on the split parameters.
signatures.safe_alternative: First confirm the absolute path and parameter boundaries. Paths containing spaces should be fully quoted, and cross-shell calls should be avoided as a priority; do not directly copy the deletion example of an unknown target.

signatures.name: Bulk changes to system directory permissions
signatures.root_cause: The command may relax the permissions of the root directory or its subdirectories in batches.
signatures.destructive_impact: If system configuration, keys, or service directories are involved, sensitive data may be exposed or services may refuse to load; the impact depends on the actual target and the success of the modification.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm that the target is limited to necessary project files, and grant the minimum permissions according to the file purpose; record the original permissions first, and do not use full recursive modification to solve local permission errors.

signatures.name: Disk management command
signatures.root_cause: Commands include formatting, file system, or partition management tools; some tools also support read-only viewing.
signatures.destructive_impact: If formatting, erasing signatures, or partition writing are actually performed, the data on the target disk may not be read normally; just starting the management tool does not mean that the disk has been cleared.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the complete parameters and target disk number, distinguish between read-only viewing and write operations; verify the backup first when writing is involved, and have the target device confirmed by the user.

signatures.name: Database or schema deletion
signatures.root_cause: Commands containing DROP DATABASE or DROP SCHEMA may delete the corresponding database objects.
signatures.destructive_impact: After successful execution, the target database or schema and its objects may be removed, and business reading and writing may be interrupted; recovery capabilities depend on the database type, transaction support, and existing backups.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the connection address, environment, and target name; back up first and verify the recovery path. Migration tools may also perform destructive operations and are not a substitute for manual inspection of migrated content.

signatures.name: Unbounded process creation
signatures.root_cause: The command contains structures that may create background processes indefinitely or recursively spawn child processes.
signatures.destructive_impact: If it continues to run, it may exhaust the process quota, memory or CPU, causing the system to become unresponsive and unsaved content to be lost; the impact is subject to resource limitations and actual execution.
signatures.safe_alternative: Stop execution and check termination conditions; verify in an isolated environment using capped concurrency pools, timeouts, and process resource limits.

signatures.name: Unauthorized transmission of credentials or environment variables
signatures.root_cause: The command attempts to directly upload files containing sensitive credentials (.env, SSH private keys, cloud vendor keys) as payloads to external URLs through network requests.
signatures.destructive_impact: It may lead to the leakage of API Keys, production database passwords or enterprise private credentials, leading to serious data leakage risks.
signatures.safe_alternative: The original credential file must never be mounted and transferred directly. If you need to test the interface, please use desensitized fake data (Mock Data).

signatures.name: Direct write to sudo permissions
signatures.root_cause: The command directly appends content to the sudoers configuration without syntax verification.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the syntax of the written content is incorrect or the permissions are inappropriate, the sudo authorization may be abnormal or the permissions may be excessively relaxed; recoverability depends on whether the management session and the original configuration are retained.
signatures.safe_alternative: Back up the configuration first, use visudo to edit or verify, and keep a valid management session until verification is completed.

signatures.name: Dynamic PowerShell execution
signatures.root_cause: The command uses Invoke-Expression or a similar method to execute a string; check whether the string comes from a remote or untrusted source.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the source of the string is not trustworthy, its content will be executed with the current user rights, which may modify files, configurations or leak credentials; using IEX alone does not prove that it has been attacked.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the actual execution string and source; the remote script first downloads, reviews and verifies the signature or trusted verification value provided by the publisher before deciding whether to run it.

signatures.name: Boot, registry, or service configuration modifications
signatures.root_cause: The command contains boot configuration, system registry or service management operations, and it needs to be confirmed whether it is actually written.
signatures.destructive_impact: Modifying critical startup or service settings may result in startup exceptions, service interruptions, or security configuration changes; read-only queries will not have these write consequences.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the specific operations and target keys, services or startup items; export relevant configurations before modification and prepare verifiable recovery steps.

signatures.name: User account or permission group changes
signatures.root_cause: The command contains characteristics of account creation or permission group member change; whether to obtain administrator permissions requires checking specific parameters.
signatures.destructive_impact: If you add a high-privilege account or expand group permissions, unintended users may access system resources; it does not mean that all account operations will create backdoors.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the account, permission group, purpose and authorizer, change according to the minimum permission, and record the status before the change.

signatures.name: Mirror synchronization may delete target files
signatures.root_cause: robocopy /MIR will keep the target directory consistent with the source directory, including deleting items in the target that are not in the source directory.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the source and target are filled in incorrectly or the source content is incomplete, unique files in the target directory may be deleted; recovery depends on backup or snapshot.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the absolute paths of the source and target, and use /L to view the planned operation first; if you only need to append the copy, do not use the mirror deletion mode.

signatures.name: Key or credential file deletion
signatures.root_cause: Removal targets involve SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other authentication files.
signatures.destructive_impact: If you delete a certificate file that is still in use, related login, deployment or automation tasks may fail; recovery depends on backup and the ability to re-issue the credentials.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the file usage and reference relationship, and first keep a protected backup or prepare for credential rotation; do not write the credential content to the log.

signatures.name: Misplaced cmd caret escape
signatures.root_cause: cmd uses ^ for escaping, with rules that differ from PowerShell and bash.
signatures.destructive_impact: Parameters are split incorrectly or commands are executed in half, which may result in accidental deletion or accidental writing to unexpected paths.
signatures.safe_alternative: Avoid nested cmd; don’t spell the cmd string if you can use PowerShell’s native writing method.

signatures.name: PowerShell collection comparison
signatures.root_cause: Comparison operations involving sets may return a set of matching elements rather than a single Boolean value.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the result is directly used to determine the deletion or migration branch, unexpected branches may be selected; the actual result depends on the operands on both sides.
signatures.safe_alternative: Make it clear whether it is an element-by-element comparison, a member check, or a quantity judgment. The result type is checked and then used to control the write operation.

signatures.name: Batch variable expansion timing
signatures.root_cause: Batch processing contains delayed expansion variables, the actual value depends on the expansion settings and statement parsing timing.
signatures.destructive_impact: The variable value may be different than expected, causing the file operation to fail or point to the wrong target; simply using an exclamation point variable does not mean that the path is necessarily empty.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check expansion settings, variable assignments, and full target paths; do not blindly enable delayed expansion when the path may contain an exclamation mark.

signatures.name: Text file encoding
signatures.root_cause: The command writes to a configuration or data file, but its encoding cannot be determined from the signature; the default encoding varies with the PowerShell version and the specific command.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the writing encoding is inconsistent with the reader's requirements, garbled characters, parsing failures, or compatibility issues may occur; not all redirections will write UTF-16.
signatures.safe_alternative: Explicitly set the encoding as required by the reader, and confirm how the current PowerShell version handles UTF-8 and BOM.

signatures.name: Recursive file operation through a link
signatures.root_cause: The command contains a recursive delete or copy parameter; this signature by itself does not prove that a link exists in the target or that the tool will follow the link.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the tool follows a join, symbolic link, or mount point, the operation may go outside the expected directory; actual behavior depends on the tool, version, and parameters.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the links and mount points in the target, and check the following behavior of the tool; preview the target range first, and do not regard parsing the real path as a separate security guarantee.

signatures.name: Windows short path
signatures.root_cause: The command contains a path that may be in 8.3 format and requires confirmation of the actual correspondence on the volume.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the short path does not exist or points to an unexpected object, the file operation may fail or act on the wrong target.
signatures.safe_alternative: First check the parsed complete long path and the target object; check that the path actually exists before performing writing.

signatures.name: Argument boundaries for paths with spaces
signatures.root_cause: A path containing spaces may be split into multiple arguments if it is not quoted correctly.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the unpacked parameters contain wildcards, copying, moving or deleting may affect additional files; the final parameters need to be checked for the specific range.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm that paths are fully referenced to avoid cross-shell splicing; check the absolute paths of all sources and targets before execution.

signatures.name: Error handling can mask failures
signatures.root_cause: The command sets silent error handling or suppresses error output, and failure information may not be visible.
signatures.destructive_impact: If a backup, migration, or cleanup step continues after a failure, subsequent writes may be based on an incomplete state.
signatures.safe_alternative: Explicitly check errors or exit statuses for key steps, record failures and stop subsequent dependent steps; external program exit codes need to be handled separately.

signatures.name: Content loaded by a system program
signatures.root_cause: The command calls a system program with scripting, component loading, or process management capabilities.
signatures.destructive_impact: If untrusted content is loaded, code may be executed with the current user's permissions; just the tool name does not confirm backdoors, persistence, or data corruption.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check loaded files, entries and sources, distinguish between read-only queries and execution operations; review untrusted content first.

signatures.name: Content downloaded by a system tool
signatures.root_cause: The command may download external content through system management tools, and you need to confirm the download source and subsequent operations.
signatures.destructive_impact: The download itself does not equal execution; subsequent loading of unverified scripts or programs may introduce untrusted code.
signatures.safe_alternative: Verify the source, placement location and subsequent execution steps; verify the file using a trusted signature or check value provided by the publisher.

signatures.name: Variable slicing, quotes, or escaping in a command
signatures.root_cause: Commands contain variable slicing, special quotes, or escape characteristics; their meaning depends on the specific shell and how they are called.
signatures.destructive_impact: If expansion or argument boundaries differ from expectations, the operation may affect the wrong target. This feature alone does not establish that injection or accidental deletion has occurred.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check which shell runs the command, the complete command text, and the final argument boundaries. Avoid concatenating untrusted input across interpreters; prefer argument arrays for separate programs.

signatures.name: Delete shadow copies
signatures.root_cause: The command requests the deletion of the specified shadow copy, and the range is determined by parameters such as volume, ID, /oldest or /all.
signatures.destructive_impact: The selected local restore points or historical versions may be lost, reducing the local recovery capability after accidental deletion; it does not mean that offline backups will also be deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: List shadow copies first and check the volume, ID, and deletion scope. Confirm a verified independent backup exists before deleting a copy.

signatures.name: Delete a backup or backup catalog
signatures.root_cause: The command requests deletion of a backup catalog or a specific backup version; catalog deletion and backup data deletion are not the same operation.
signatures.destructive_impact: Deleting a catalog may make existing backups difficult to locate through the current catalog; deleting a backup version will remove the corresponding recovery point, the actual impact depends on the subcommand.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the subcommand and backup version, then retain and verify an independent backup. For catalog problems, first consider restoring or reimporting the catalog; catalog deletion does not invalidate every backup.

signatures.name: Bulk changes to file ownership or permissions
signatures.root_cause: Commands may recursively change file owners or ACLs, depending on the account, permissions, and inheritance settings.
signatures.destructive_impact: If permissions are extended to unintended accounts, sensitive files may be exposed; if permissions are revoked by mistake, application or management operations may fail, and permissions may not necessarily be granted to all users.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the absolute target, account and recursive scope, and save the restorable permission configuration first; only modify the minimum permissions for necessary directories.

signatures.name: Disk partition write operation
signatures.root_cause: The command or diskpart script may include write operations such as clean, format, or delete partitions.
signatures.destructive_impact: The partition or file system structure of the target disk may be modified, making the original data inaccessible; continuing to write may reduce the chance of recovery.
signatures.safe_alternative: Review the complete script, disk number, and capacity to distinguish a write from a read-only query. Verify a backup before writing; after an accidental write, stop writing to the device immediately.

signatures.name: Delete registry key
signatures.root_cause: Command requests deletion of a registry key or value; /f usually omits confirmation, the actual effect is determined by the target key.
signatures.destructive_impact: The target configuration may be lost, and related applications, services, or startup items may malfunction. A registry deletion does not always prevent startup.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the complete key path, value name and purpose, and export the target configuration first; avoid unreviewed batch deletion of system keys.

signatures.name: Overwrite disk free space
signatures.root_cause: cipher /w will overwrite the available space of the specified volume to reduce the recoverability of deleted data.
signatures.destructive_impact: The chance of recovery of deleted file remnants may be reduced; this operation is not an ordinary cache cleanup, nor does it mean that the files in use are directly deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm that secure erasure is indeed required rather than freeing space; first confirm the target volume and backup, and do not perform it on volumes that need to recover accidentally deleted data.

signatures.name: Securely wipe files or free space
signatures.root_cause: The actual behavior of SDelete is determined by the file target and free space cleaning options.
signatures.destructive_impact: Selected files or remaining free areas may be overwritten, reducing the chance of recovery; whether free space is involved depends on the options, and complete erasure of all storage media cannot be guaranteed.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the file path and erasure options, and keep necessary backups first. Ordinary Remove-Item also usually does not go through the Recycle Bin, so it cannot be treated as reversibly deleted.

signatures.name: Clear event log
signatures.root_cause: The command contains an operation to clear the Windows event log; modifying the log configuration should be checked separately from the clearing operation.
signatures.destructive_impact: Selected local event records may be lost, affecting troubleshooting and auditing; remotely collected or exported records may not be affected.
signatures.safe_alternative: First export the logs that need to be retained, and confirm the target logs and authorizations; when troubleshooting, give priority to querying the logs rather than clearing the records.

signatures.name: Delete NTFS change log
signatures.root_cause: The command requests deletion of the USN change log for the target volume.
signatures.destructive_impact: Existing file change records for the volume may be unavailable, affecting USN-dependent indexing, backup, or investigation; this does not mean that all audit records have been deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the target volume and USN-dependent services, and keep necessary records first; give priority to read-only queries when troubleshooting.

signatures.name: Delete a local Time Machine snapshot
signatures.root_cause: The command requests the deletion of a selected local snapshot or a snapshot of a volume.
signatures.destructive_impact: The corresponding local recovery points may be lost; the availability of other snapshots and external Time Machine backups needs to be confirmed separately.
signatures.safe_alternative: List the snapshots first and confirm the specific volumes or time points, and then clean up after verifying that the external backup is recoverable.

signatures.name: Read sensitive keychain content
signatures.root_cause: The command requests to export keychain information or read passwords; what can be read depends on subcommands, permissions, and system authorizations.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the output contains passwords or keys, the terminal, logs, or subsequent uploads may reveal the credentials; tool calls alone cannot be used to conclude that all credentials have been compromised.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the specific entries read and user authorization, and do not write sensitive output to logs or upload; prioritize access using controlled credentials supported by the system.

signatures.name: Delete application or global preferences
signatures.root_cause: defaults delete removes a specified preference domain or key; the scope depends on the domain, key, and options such as -g.
signatures.destructive_impact: Corresponding preferences may be restored to default or cause application behavior to change; this does not mean that all network, security and system settings will be lost together.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the target domain and key, and export relevant preferences first; only delete items that clearly need to be reset.

signatures.name: Remove extended attributes
signatures.root_cause: xattr removes or clears extended attributes, which may include a quarantine attribute affecting downloaded files.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the quarantine mark is removed, the system's inspection path for the downloaded content may change; other extended attributes may also be lost, but deleting the attributes itself is not equivalent to executing the program.
signatures.safe_alternative: Inspect the existing attributes and target files. Verify the source, signature, and purpose of downloaded content; clearing attributes in bulk is no substitute for that review.

signatures.name: Deactivate LaunchAgent or LaunchDaemon
signatures.root_cause: The launchctl command requests to uninstall, deactivate, or remove a specified service. The service domain and identity need to be confirmed.
signatures.destructive_impact: The target service may stop or no longer start automatically; this only affects these functions if the target is part of a monitoring or backup component.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the service purpose, operating domain and dependencies, record the original status and recovery commands; do not confuse user services with system services.

signatures.name: Bulk deletion with find
signatures.root_cause: find will delete the objects in the starting directory that satisfy the expression or call the delete program.
signatures.destructive_impact: Matched files may be deleted without going through the Recycle Bin; if the starting point or filtering conditions are wrong, the deletion scope may exceed expectations, and unbacked content may be difficult to recover.
signatures.safe_alternative: List the matching targets first using a consistent starting point and filter conditions. Note that -delete implies depth-first traversal and expression order; check the linking strategy, scope and backup before deciding.

signatures.name: Write directly to disk device
signatures.root_cause: The dd output may be a disk or partition device; arguments determine the write position and length.
signatures.destructive_impact: Overwriting a partition table, file system metadata, or file contents may corrupt target data. A dd write does not necessarily erase an entire disk.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the output device, offset, and write length, and verify the backup. Use a bounded disk image for development; after an accidental write, stop writing to the device.

signatures.name: dd overwrites an existing file
signatures.root_cause: The dd output path is in the configuration, log, or user directory; whether to overwrite and write content is determined by the input and conversion parameters.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the target file already contains content, it may be truncated or overwritten, causing damage to configuration, logs or user data; it may not be cleared.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check input, output, and truncation options, and back up existing targets first; do not use direct overwrites as a substitute for auditable configuration changes or log rotation.

signatures.name: Recreate a file system or swap area
signatures.root_cause: The command may create a file system or swap area on the target device, and you need to distinguish between actual writing and preview options.
signatures.destructive_impact: Actual writing may replace the original metadata, making the data in the target partition inaccessible; recovery depends on the writing range and backup.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the device, purpose, and whether the arguments are read-only; verify the backup. For debugging, use a dedicated test image instead of a production disk.

signatures.name: Archive tool runs an external command
signatures.root_cause: The tar argument contains options for checkpointing or passing the contents to an external command for processing.
signatures.destructive_impact: The archiving operation may additionally execute the specified command or pass the file content to it; if the handler is not trustworthy, the data may be modified or the content may be leaked.
signatures.safe_alternative: Review the external program, arguments, and input source. Remove execution callbacks when only packing or unpacking is needed. --to-command also executes an external program and is not a safe substitute.

signatures.name: Inline interpreter script
signatures.root_cause: The command executes the script through the inline option of the interpreter such as Python, Node, Perl, etc.
signatures.destructive_impact: The script runs with the current user’s permissions. Its contents determine whether it deletes files, starts processes, or accesses the network; inline syntax alone does not indicate malicious behavior.
signatures.safe_alternative: Read the complete script to check file, network and subprocess operations and input sources; changing to a script file facilitates review, but does not in itself reduce permissions or eliminate risks.

signatures.name: Encoded PowerShell script
signatures.root_cause: PowerShell commands are passed into scripts via encoded parameters, which are encoded for transport rather than secure isolation.
signatures.destructive_impact: The actual execution content is not intuitive in the command line; if not reviewed, file modifications, downloads, or access to sensitive information may be missed. Encoding alone does not prove malicious behavior.
signatures.safe_alternative: Decode the command using PowerShell’s expected encoding without executing it. Review the decoded text and its source before deciding whether to run it.

signatures.name: Download content directly to the interpreter
signatures.root_cause: The output of the network request is piped directly to the shell or other interpreter.
signatures.destructive_impact: Remote content will be executed with the current user's permissions; if the source is tampered with or the script exceeds expectations, files or configuration may be modified, or credentials leaked.
signatures.safe_alternative: Download and review the content first, verify it using the publisher's trusted signature or checksum; confirm the source and required permissions before running it explicitly.

signatures.name: Force push a Git branch
signatures.root_cause: git push uses the force update option to allow non-fast forward updates to remote references.
signatures.destructive_impact: A remote branch may be overwritten by local history, and other people's commits may no longer appear on that branch; whether the commit object is still recoverable depends on other references, retention periods, and backups.
signatures.safe_alternative: Fetch first and check the remote differences; if you really need to rewrite, confirm the clear expected remote commit, use --force-with-lease with the expected value, and comply with branch protection and collaboration agreements.

signatures.name: Git hard reset
signatures.root_cause: git reset --hard resets tracked files in the index and workspace to the target commit.
signatures.destructive_impact: Uncommitted changes to tracked files may be discarded; specifying old commits may also move branch pointers, and untracked files that are blocking writes may be deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Review the status first and save the actual file changes; stash -u includes untracked files but does not include ignored files. Ignored files need to be backed up separately. Merely creating a backup branch cannot protect uncommitted changes.

signatures.name: Git clean deletes untracked files
signatures.root_cause: git clean requests the deletion of untracked files; whether directories and ignored files are included depends on the -d, -x and other options respectively.
signatures.destructive_impact: Source files, local configurations, or artifacts that have not yet been put into version control may be deleted; Git generally cannot recover content that was never recorded, and external backups or editor histories may still have copies.
signatures.safe_alternative: Perform a dry-run preview using the same scope and options as the planned deletion, for example -fdx versus -ndx; back up untracked and ignored files that need to be retained first, and then specify the path explicitly.

signatures.name: Forcefully delete a Git branch
signatures.root_cause: The command bypasses the merged check and deletes the specified local branch reference.
signatures.destructive_impact: If the branch is the only reference to certain commits, those commits may be more difficult to locate and may not be recoverable after subsequent cleanup; deleting the reference does not mean immediately deleting the commit object.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check whether the branch is merged, record its head commit, and retain any needed reference. Use ordinary branch deletion when possible.

signatures.name: Prune unused Docker resources
signatures.root_cause: The command requests cleaning of unused containers, networks, images, or build caches; --volumes additionally refers to unused anonymous volumes, and volume rm targets explicitly specified volumes.
signatures.destructive_impact: The cleaned resources may need to be recreated; if they contain volumes that hold necessary data, the data in the volumes may be lost. Not all volumes will be deleted, nor will active databases be cleared directly.
signatures.safe_alternative: Review the complete options and resources to be removed. Check whether volumes contain needed data and back them up first. -a broadens the unused image scope, while -f skips confirmation; -f alone does not imply volume deletion.

signatures.name: Bulk deletion of Kubernetes resources
signatures.root_cause: kubectl delete --all requests deletion of the selected resource type in the selected scope.
signatures.destructive_impact: Target workloads may stop. Deleting a namespace may also delete its PVCs; whether persistent data is lost depends on the storage reclaim policy. The all resource category does not include every cluster resource.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the current context, namespace, and resource type, then list the intended targets. For PVCs, check backups and the PV reclaim policy; use an applicable dry run when needed.

signatures.name: Terraform destroy with automatic approval
signatures.root_cause: terraform destroy -auto-approve skips interactive confirmation and destroys resources according to the current status and configuration plan.
signatures.destructive_impact: Resources managed by the target workspace may be deleted, and services may be interrupted. Whether data can be recovered depends on the resource type, protection settings, and backup. It does not mean that all resources in the account will be deleted.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the account, backend, and workspace, then review terraform plan -destroy. Remove -auto-approve and verify backups and deletion protection; production deletion needs human authorization.

signatures.name: Delete a cloud storage bucket or object
signatures.root_cause: The command requests a bucket deletion or object deletion recursively, with the actual scope determined by the target URL and options.
signatures.destructive_impact: Selected buckets or objects may be removed, disrupting services that rely on them. Recovery depends on soft deletion, version retention, retention policies, and independent backups.
signatures.safe_alternative: Check the project, bucket, and object prefixes, and list the target and protection settings first; confirm that there are available backups before authorizing deletion. Lifecycle rules also need to review the deletion scope.

signatures.name: Delete a virtual machine snapshot
signatures.root_cause: The command requests the removal of one or more snapshots of the specified virtual machine; remove has a different scope than removeall.
signatures.destructive_impact: The corresponding snapshot rollback point may be lost, and merging snapshots may also cause additional I/O or space pressure; this does not mean deleting the current data of the virtual machine.
signatures.safe_alternative: Confirm the VM ID, snapshot range, and independent backup, and check the space required for consolidation; do not rely on snapshots as the only backup.

signatures.name: Recursive or forced file deletion
signatures.root_cause: The target path, wildcards, and recursion flags determine the deletion scope; force may suppress confirmation or ignore some errors.
signatures.destructive_impact: Specified files or directory contents may be deleted without going through the Recycle Bin; if paths, variables, or wildcard expansions are incorrect, unexpected files may be affected, and unbacked contents may be difficult to recover.
signatures.safe_alternative: First check the absolute target path and the matching files, confirm that they are in the expected directory and back up the necessary content. PowerShell can use -LiteralPath to avoid wildcard interpretation and use -WhatIf preview; rm does not have a general dry-run, so do not execute it directly to verify the range.

signatures.name: Deletion target may be root or a user home directory
signatures.root_cause: The deletion target belongs to a wide range of directories, or may be wildcard expanded into multiple top-level targets.
signatures.destructive_impact: If actually executed and permissions are allowed, a large number of system or user files may be deleted, resulting in abnormal application, login or system operation; GNU rm protects the root directory / by default, but this protection cannot be considered to cover all wildcards or other implementations.
signatures.safe_alternative: Pause deletion and check the complete absolute target and expansion scope. If you are just clearing the cache, change it to a clear cache directory within the project, and confirm the file list and backup first; do not turn off root directory protection to continue execution.
